title: Passover: four children
hook: the wise, the wicked, the simple, and the one who doesn't know how to ask
tomorrow: Passover: it would have been enough

segments.voice: Yesterday, the seder plate, where every item tells part of the story. Your line was every item speaks. Today, the people the story is told to.

Anyone who's explained something to a room knows this moment. You've told the story, and now the questions come. One person asks something sharp and detailed. One rolls their eyes: why does anyone bother? One just says, wait, what is this? And one says nothing at all, and you can't tell if they're lost or bored or shy. The Torah tells parents four separate times to explain the Exodus to a child. The rabbis noticed the four verses don't match, and from that they built a whole page of the Haggadah, the book read at the seder.
screen: `ONE SHARP, ONE SCORNFUL.` → `ONE CONFUSED, ONE SILENT.` → `FOUR VERSES THAT DON'T MATCH.`

segments.voice: The Haggadah says the Torah speaks of four children: one wise, one wicked, one simple, and one who doesn't know how to ask. Each gets a different answer. The wise child asks about all the testimonies, statutes and laws God commanded, so you teach them the laws of Passover, down to the last detail of the night. The wicked child asks, what is this service to you? To you, the Haggadah notices, not to him. He's stepped out of the circle, so the answer is blunt, a verse in the old Jewish translation: "It is because of that which the LORD did for me when I came forth out of Egypt." For me, not for him. Strong words, and Jewish teachers have argued about them for centuries. Many say the point is that even this child is at the table, and still gets an answer. The simple child asks, what is this? So you answer simply: with a strong hand, God brought us out of Egypt, from the house of slavery. And the one who doesn't know how to ask? You open it up for them. You start the conversation. In the Hebrew, that you is feminine, at, and some take it as a hint that this child is often helped first by a mother. The page gives no single right way to tell the story. You tell it to the person in front of you, at their level. Four children, four answers, one table.
screen: `FOUR CHILDREN, FOUR ANSWERS.` · `THE WISE: ALL THE LAWS.` · `THE WICKED: FOR ME, NOT HIM.` · `THE SILENT: YOU OPEN IT UP.` · then, large: `ANSWER EACH CHILD.`

segments.voice: Think of someone who asked you something lately: a child, a coworker, a friend new to something you know well. Were they sharp, skeptical, confused or silent? Picture answering them again at their level: more detail, fewer words, or a door opened for the question they didn't know to ask.
Passover. The festival of leaving Egypt, and a story told four ways, to four children. Today's word.
Your line: answer each child. A week of things turned upside down: two gifts, masks, clearing out, a candle, a plate that speaks, and four children. That's day six hundred seventy-nine.

screen: `DAY 679 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: PASSOVER: IT WOULD HAVE BEEN ENOUGH.`

howItsDone: At the seder, after the Four Questions, the Haggadah's passage of the four children is read aloud, and many families discuss it, sometimes using illustrated Haggadot that picture the four children in very different ways.

chat.says: Why does the Haggadah give four children four different answers?
options: Each one asks differently, so you answer each at their own level.
Only the wise child gets a real answer; the others are brushed off.
Each answer is meant for a different night of the holiday.
chat.meaning: The Haggadah sets four children at the table and answers each at their own level, even opening the story for the one who can't ask.

notes: Audit (y2 second sample): removed stock lines ('one of the most famous pages', 'a small detail many people love', 'the deepest lesson of the page is simple').
Exodus 13:8 quoted from JPS 1917 from memory; verify.
The Haggadah's answers paraphrased; the wise child's answer ('no afikoman after the Passover offering') is summarized as 'the last detail of the night'.
Mekhilta Bo 18 and Yerushalmi Pesachim 10:4 have variant versions; verify reference.
The feminine 'at' in 'at p'tach lo' and the reading that it hints at a mother is a popular homily; labeled 'some take it'.
Haggadah calls them 'four sons' (arba'ah banim); 'children' used here as many modern Haggadot do.
